---
title: "Grants as code: compiled budgets, funder views, and machine-checkable applications"
author:
  - name: Max Ghenis
    affiliations: [PolicyEngine, The Axiom Foundation]
date: 2026-08-14
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
abstract: >
  Grant applications are assembled by hand from three kinds of material that
  organizations already hold in structured form: the work they intend to do,
  the cost of the people and systems that do it, and the rules of the funder's
  form. We describe a pipeline that treats each as data — a priced menu of
  work items with machine-checkable completion evidence; personnel rates
  derived from encoded tax and retirement law with benchmark provenance;
  funder proposals as selections over the shared menu, with co-funding
  fractions that make cross-application double-billing a pre-award,
  machine-checked invariant; and versioned funder packs that validate and
  assemble the application in continuous integration. A six-lane landscape
  review adjudicates what is new. The pre-award cross-application gate is
  novel as a machine check, though the invariant it enforces is old federal
  policy. Funder-as-view is novel as a mechanism, with named ancestors that
  reuse by copying forward rather than by constrained views. The
  funder-facing configurator is novel, with the thinnest neighbor set of the
  six claims. Budget compilation and rule-derived rates are partially
  anticipated — closed rate-table engines and payroll calculators exist —
  and survive only in their precise forms. Closed funder-side validation
  already runs at scale in NIH ASSIST; the contribution here is open,
  versioned, applicant-side, funder-portable rule packs — a domain transfer
  of the compliance-as-code pattern. The engine and schemas are open source;
  the reference rates provider's public release is pending.
---

# The claims {#sec-claims}

The paper stands or falls on six claims. Each was tested adversarially
against six tool lanes: a research pass was instructed to kill any claim
with prior art, and its verdicts appear in brackets after each claim, argued
in full in @sec-landscape.

**C1 — Budgets as compiled artifacts.** A grant budget should be the output
of a pure function over (menu items, rates, selection), reproducible in CI,
not a spreadsheet edited toward a total. Changing a rate or a selection
regenerates every downstream table identically — in the proposal document,
the funder deck, and the org's public planning pages. [Verdict: partial
prior art. Rate-table budget engines and structured cost buildup exist,
closed or — where once open — frozen since 2017. We concede the loose form,
"computing budgets from data"; the claim survives only as stated: pure
function, work-item menu, reproducible in CI.]

**C2 — The pre-award double-billing gate.** When proposals are selections
with per-item co-funding fractions, "no item is more than 100% funded across
simultaneous applications" becomes a machine-checked invariant at draft time.
Federal post-award machinery (2 CFR 200 effort certification) attests this
retrospectively and manually; we know of no pre-award, automatic equivalent.
[Verdict: novel as a machine check. The invariant itself is old federal
policy, and every pre-award enforcement found is human review of
self-reported forms; the novelty is enforcement timing plus automation.]

**C3 — Rule-derived personnel rates.** Loaded personnel costs computed from
encoded law — employer payroll taxes by jurisdiction, retirement contribution
caps (IRS §415(c)/§402(g)), benefit schedules — rather than flat multipliers,
with market benchmarks (BLS OES, sourced percentiles) attached per role. The
budget's comp-justification appendix becomes a generated artifact. [Verdict:
partial prior art. The computation exists in payroll engines and web
calculators; the benchmarks exist as data products. We concede the loose
form, "computing employer burden from rules"; what was not found is the
composition — statutory loading plus benchmark provenance in a citable,
pre-award rate object inside a budget compilation.]

**C4 — Funder-as-view.** One organizational substrate (the menu), many
proposals as selections over it. The org maintains its work-item database
once; each funder sees a view: selected items, fractions, an org-base
allocation, a window. Views make co-funding legible instead of narrative.
[Verdict: novel as a mechanism. The ancestors — basis-of-estimate libraries,
shared data commons, common applications, braided-funding practice — all
reuse by copying forward (estimates, text, data); none constrains N live
proposals as fractional views over one priced substrate.]

**C5 — Funder packs: the application as a checked build.** Funder form rules
— section structure, word/character/page limits, budget caps, required
attachments, placeholder gates — as versioned code; the application repo
builds in CI to a status artifact and an assembled document. (Shipped in
grantkit 0.2.x; @sec-pipeline.) [Verdict: the core exists at scale, closed —
NIH ASSIST validates against encoded business rules and reports itemized
errors and warnings. What remains, and what we claim, is the open,
versioned, applicant-side, funder-portable packaging with a repo-resident
status artifact — the compliance-as-code pattern carried into a new domain.]

**C6 — The configurator.** Because budgets compile (C1), a funder can be
handed the model itself: presets and toggles over the same menu and rates the
organization runs on, every configuration inside adjudicated bounds. Scenario
pressure-testing becomes something the funder does live, not a static
appendix. [Verdict: novel, with the thinnest neighbor set of the six —
and funder adoption is untested beyond one live diligence (@sec-case).]

The through-line — and the paper's one-sentence thesis: **the grant pipeline
inherits the properties of the software pipeline the moment its inputs become
data: reproducibility, diffability, invariants checked before submission
instead of audited after award.**

# Landscape {#sec-landscape}

We swept six tool lanes on 2026-08-14 — vendor documentation, help centers,
and federal guidance, discounting marketing claims where the docs said less —
with an adversarial brief: find prior art that kills each claim. One caveat
governs everything that follows: the sweep was US-centric and
English-language, so a verdict of *novel* means no prior art found, not
proven absent.

## Applicant-side writing tools

Does any grant-writing tool derive budgets from structured work-item data?
The finding: they draft narrative text and track awards; none compiles a
budget from a work-item substrate. The closest thing to budget generation in
this lane is a language model writing a budget-shaped table as prose.

[Instrumentl](https://www.instrumentl.com/product-overview) pairs grant
discovery with tracking and post-award management; its budget feature,
[Budget Spenddown Tracking](https://help.instrumentl.com/en/articles/9114092-budget-spenddown-tracking),
takes a funder-approved award budget, extracts its categories, syncs actuals
from accounting, and alerts on over- and under-spend — post-award and
expense-side. [Grantable](https://grantable.co/) runs
[AI drafting over a content library](https://www.grantable.co/features/ai-grant-writing-assistant)
— write once, reuse across proposals — a narrative cousin of C4's substrate,
with no budget model, no fractions, no checks.
[Granted AI](https://grantedai.com/features) matches funders from
990-derived profiles, analyzes RFPs, drafts section by section, and
simulates a six-reviewer committee; budget appears only as interview
questions that ground the narrative, and the committee is stochastic
critique, not machine-checkable validation. FreeWill's
[Grant Assistant](https://www.nonprofits.freewill.com/products/grant-assistant)
is the lane's nearest neighbor to C5: it generates a requirements matrix
from the RFP and scans the proposal against it to catch gaps before
submission — but the matrix is model-generated per proposal, not a
versioned, citable rule pack, and the check is advisory prose, not a
deterministic exit code.
[Streamline](https://streamlineclimate.com/solutions/startup) runs an AI
grant and RFP pipeline for climate applicants — opportunity search,
solicitation summarization, drafting, reuse — narrative only.
[Grantboost](https://www.grantboost.io/nonprofits/) generates proposals from
a survey and honors per-section word and character limits: the germ of a
funder rule, with no encoded pack, no lint, no artifact. Submittable's
applicant side fills funder-built web forms behind
[eligibility screeners](https://submittable.help/en/articles/3872413-eligibility-forms)
with required-field and type validation — machine gating exists, but the
rules live inside the funder's portal, invisible and unversioned from the
applicant's side. [OpenGrants](https://opengrants.io/for-grant-seekers/),
despite the name, is open *data access* — a search engine over 70k+
listings, a grant-writer marketplace, and a REST API — not open-source
tooling. And a genre of free prompt tools, represented by LogicBalls'
[AI grant budget template](https://logicballs.com/tools/grant-budget-template),
has a model write the budget table from a project description: C1's contrast
in its purest form, a budget as generated text that re-running does not
reproduce.

The lane kills nothing. Its strongest neighbor is Grant Assistant's
requirements matrix — C5-adjacent and non-deterministic.

## Funder-side grants management

Does any grants management system expose applicant-side budget composition,
or validation the applicant can hold? All of them validate form fields and
workflow state; none sees inside the applicant's cost model, and none checks
allocation across a portfolio of applications to other funders.

[Fluxx Grantmaker](https://www.fluxx.io/products/grantmaker-fluxx-grants-management-software)
gives funders configurable forms and workflows, a grantee portal, budget and
finance tracking of awards, and automated validation steps — required
fields, data standardization — all portal-side and per-form, with budgets as
attachments and line tables.
[Foundant GLM](https://www.foundant.com/products/grant-management-software-for-foundations/)
runs application through review, payment, and follow-up for small and
mid-size foundations, with a branching form builder and budgets tracked as
program-level allocations drawn down by payments.
[Submittable's funder side](https://www.submittable.com/features/online-forms)
builds forms, gates eligibility, stages review, and validates applicant data
against third-party databases.
[SmartSimple Cloud](https://www.smartsimple.com/solution/grants-management-tracking-software)
adds eligibility quizzes, IRS and watchlist vetting, and a Budget Manager
whose business rules drive funder-side budget and payment schedules — rules
that govern the funder's payments, not the applicant's budget composition.
Salesforce grantmaking spans the free, open-source
[Outbound Funds Module](https://appexchange.salesforce.com/appxListingDetail?listingId=a0N3A00000G5vDxUAJ)
— funding programs, requests, disbursements, expenditures — and the
commercial Nonprofit Cloud for Grantmaking; notable as the lane's one
open-source artifact, it models money movement, not application content or
budget derivation.
[Blackbaud Grantmaking](https://webfiles-sc1.blackbaud.com/files/support/helpfiles/grantmaking/content/budget-phase1.html)
manages funder budget hierarchies — categories, reserve funds, line items —
with payment appropriation controls and, since 2024, an applicant portal
with an AI form builder; the budget machinery is entirely funder-internal.
[WizeHive Zengine](https://softwareconnect.com/reviews/wizehive-zengine/) is
a flexible form, review, and workflow builder for grants, scholarships, and
awards. [AmpliFund](https://www.amplifund.com/features/) comes closest to
budget mechanics, tracking budgets, indirect costs, and staff hours through
the award lifecycle for governments that receive and pass through funds —
still award tracking, not proposal compilation.

The lane sharpens C5 rather than killing it: machine validation of
applications is ubiquitous inside closed funder portals, so the novelty left
is applicant-side, versioned, open, funder-portable rule packs with a
repo-resident status artifact.

## Nonprofit budgeting and finance

Does anything gate multi-funder allocation before award? Multi-funder
allocation turns out to be a solved *post-award accounting* problem and a
supported *budget-planning* feature; nothing gates allocation across
simultaneous, not-yet-awarded proposals.

[Sage Intacct's grants tracking and billing](https://www.sage.com/en-us/sage-business-cloud/intacct/product-capabilities/extended-capabilities/grants-tracking-billing/)
allocates expenses to grants across payables, purchasing, ledger, expenses,
and timesheets; bills indirect costs at negotiated, specific, or markup
rates; tracks employee effort per grant from timesheets; and flags
unallowable spend against budget. This is how double-charging is actually
prevented today: after award, expense by expense, by bookkeeping discipline.
It is also a C3 contrast — indirect and fringe are configured rates, not
law. [Martus](https://www.martussolutions.com/capabilities/personnel) is the
lane's nearest neighbor to C2 and C4: its personnel budgeting supports an
employee funded by multiple grants, allocated by hours, amount, or
percentage, by month or year. A person split across grants by percentage is
the same object as a co-funding fraction — but Martus is an internal
planning worksheet for known or expected funding: no notion of simultaneous
pending applications, no constraint that fractions across open proposals sum
to at most one, no machine gate, no artifact a funder sees.
[Limelight](https://www.golimelight.com/industries/non-profit) has the same
shape — nonprofit FP&A templates for grants, funds, programs, and workforce
planning. On the free end, Propel Nonprofits'
[True Program Costs template](https://propelnonprofits.org/resources/true-program-costs-program-budget-and-allocation-template-and-resource/)
is the sector's state of the art for budget-from-structure: a spreadsheet
with formulas — computed, but not versioned, testable, or reproducible
outside the workbook. The Wallace Foundation's
[StrongNonprofits toolkit](https://wallacefoundation.org/toolkit/strongnonprofits-toolkit?s=budgeting)
ships a
[Program-Based Budget Builder](https://wallacefoundation.org/sites/default/files/2023-10/program-based-budget-builder-overview.pdf)
that allocates personnel and shared costs to programs, and an
out-of-school-time cost calculator that "works like a mortgage calculator" —
a genuine closed-form cost model exposed to planners, and so a C6 ancestor,
but built on generic benchmarks rather than the org's own live model, and
not aimed at funder diligence. Indirect-cost practice itself is a C3
contrast: 2 CFR 200's de minimis rate (10%, raised to 15% in the 2024 OMB
revision) or a negotiated NICRA, implemented in budgets as a multiplier row
— the compliance apparatus standardizes *multipliers*, which is exactly what
C3 replaces with computed statutory costs. And the
[fund-accounting validation genre](https://www.criadv.com/insight/managing-restricted-funds/)
— Aplos, MIP, FastFund — prevents charging the wrong fund and distributes
expenses across funds on entry: the don't-bill-twice invariant, in
production software, post-award and expense-by-expense.

The lane establishes that the ≤100% allocation object exists in planning
tools (Martus) and the double-charging invariant exists in accounting tools
(Intacct et al.) — both outside the pre-award window.

## Federal compliance machinery

What exists for cross-application allocation checking, and is any of it
pre-award and automatic? The rule — no more than 100% commitment, no
double-charging — is old and explicit. Its enforcement is human at every
pre-award point we found. Budget arithmetic and form validation, by
contrast, are heavily automated — inside closed systems.

Effort certification is the incumbent answer to cross-source personnel
allocation.
[Huron ECC](https://www.huronconsultinggroup.com/-/media/Resource-Media-Content/Education/research-suite/Huron-Research-Suite-Employee-Compensation-Compliance.pdf),
née ecrt, dominates university compliance with 2 CFR 200.430: it
[generates effort and payroll statements](https://finance.uw.edu/pafc/effort-reporting/ecc-system/ecc-overview)
that principal investigators certify *after the fact*, as traditional effort
reporting or project-based payroll confirmation.
[Maximus ERS](https://maximus.com/specialized-markets/higher-ed/effort-reporting-system-and-services)
is the same category — web-based, after-the-fact certification with
escalation workflows. Both are strong evidence *for* C2's novelty: the
incumbent solution is post-award attestation, workflow-managed but
substantively human.

The policy layer for C2 is current-and-pending support. NIH's
[Grants Policy Statement §2.5.1](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/policy/nihgps/HTML5/section_2/2.5.1_just-in-time_procedures.htm)
does not permit commitment overlap — more than 100% or twelve person-months
across all support — and resolves it "with the applicant and the PD/PI at
the time of award": staff read just-in-time submissions and negotiate
([UW–Madison's summary](https://rsp.wisc.edu/other-support-information.cfm)).
University pre-award offices review the forms so listed effort sums
correctly (e.g.,
[Tufts OVPR guidance](https://viceprovost.tufts.edu/policies-forms-guides/current-and-pending-other-support-proposals-and-awards)).
[NSF's current-and-pending FAQ](https://www.nsf.gov/funding/senior-personnel-documents/faq/current-pending)
describes using the data to assess overcommitment, with no automated check.
We found no agency system that automatically sums commitments across
applications; the guidance uniformly describes staff review. This is the
closest practice to C2 anywhere: the constraint is standard, the machine
gate absent.

[NIH ASSIST and the eRA validations](https://www.era.nih.gov/about-era/other-services/validations)
are the strongest single prior art against C5. Applications are validated
against "many NIH business rules" before submission; errors block
submission, warnings do not; failures produce an
[itemized errors-and-warnings results page](https://www.era.nih.gov/erahelp/assist/Content/ASSIST_Help_Topics/5_Preview_Print_Submit/Submit_Validated_Application.htm).
Free to applicants, closed system. What it is not: open, versioned,
applicant-side, or portable — the rules are opaque implementation, the
artifact is a transient results page, and coverage is federal NIH-family
forms.

[Grants.gov Workspace](https://www.grants.gov/applicants/encountering-error-messages.html)
documents "Check for Errors" and Check Application runs that validate fields
and cross-form consistency — budget totals must reconcile between SF-424A
detail and summary — before submission. Its
[system-to-system pages](https://www.grants.gov/system-to-system/grantor-system-to-system/schemas)
publish versioned XML schemas for opportunity and application handling
(GrantsCommonTypes-V1.0, GrantsCommonElements-V1.0,
ApplicantCommonElements-V1.0, GrantsFundingSynopsis-V2.0); the
[forms repository](https://grants.gov/forms/forms-repository/sf-424-family)
serves the SF-424 family as sample PDFs marked not submittable, and we did
not confirm per-form XSDs on the public pages. Partial prior art for C5's
"form rules as code": federal system-to-system interchange is literally
versioned schema, but per-form business rules and caps are only partly
encoded, the validator is a hosted black box, and nothing lands in the
applicant's repo.

[Cayuse 424](https://support.cayuse.com/hc/en-us/articles/115013731528)
builds system-to-system proposals with a running errors-warnings-info list
replicating Grants.gov and agency validations, and
[auto-calculates budgets](https://support.cayuse.com/hc/en-us/articles/115013737108-Adding-Fringe-Rates-and-Benefits-in-Proposals-S2S)
from institutional profiles — fringe rate tables, 3% inflation escalation,
1% yearly fringe drift, F&A averaged across fiscal years. That is prior art
against C5 (live validation with severity levels) and against C1's weak form
(budgets computed from structured inputs and rate tables). What is missing
for C1 proper: the inputs are cost categories and rates, not a work-item
menu; the computation is interactive and stateful, not a pure function; and
nothing reproduces outside the vendor system.
[Kuali Research's budget engine](https://kuali-research.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/115010656047-Proposal-Budget-Budget-Engine-Calculations)
is the same shape — institutional rate tables driving automatic calculation
"on a precise daily calculation," with cost share and unrecovered F&A — and
the sharpest C3 contrast in the wild: fringe is *defined* as salary times a
configured rate; no one computes it from statute. Kuali is also not simply
closed: the engine descends from MIT's Coeus through Kuali Coeus, community
source under the Educational Community License from 2006, spun off
for-profit in 2014; the open-source ancestor
([github.com/kuali/kc](https://github.com/kuali/kc), AGPL-3.0) remains
public but frozen since January 2017, and the current commercial engine is
closed.

The closest pre-award multi-funder allocation practice found anywhere is the
Advance Planning Document regime in state health and human services systems.
[45 CFR 95.610](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/95.610) requires
states to submit APDs with a proposed budget and "an estimate of the
prospective cost allocation/distribution to the various State and Federal
funding sources" *before* acquiring systems;
[CMS](https://www.medicaid.gov/federal-policy-guidance/downloads/faq061319.pdf)
and [ACF](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocse/apd_guide_2.pdf)
fund at enhanced matching rates (90/75/50) and publish cost-allocation
methodology toolkits, and multi-program APDs cover systems funded by several
federal programs at once. Conceptually this is C2 plus C4 — one system,
several funders, declared shares, approval before spend. The implementation
is narrative documents, spreadsheet methodologies, and human federal
reviewers: no machine check, no code, no reproducibility. We cite it as the
manual ancestor.

Finally, [SF-424A](https://grants.gov/forms/forms-repository/sf-424-family)
itself — the government-wide budget form, with Section A and B matrices by
object class and funding source and totals that must reconcile, its tooling
a fillable PDF plus the validators above — is the C1 contrast in one object:
the canonical grant budget is a *form*, downstream of whatever spreadsheet
produced the numbers, and provenance ends at data entry.

The lane wounds C5 (validation with status reporting exists at scale,
closed) and C1's weak form (rate-table budget engines exist, closed); it
strengthens C2 and supplies C4's manual ancestor.

## Docs-as-code and policy-as-code

Who already owns the pattern — documents plus rules plus CI plus status
artifacts — and has anyone pointed it at grants? The pattern is mature in
adjacent domains. The exact phrases return nothing: no tool, paper, or
product styled "grants as code" or "CI for grants" was found for grant
applications in the 2026-08 sweep (results are license and crypto noise).

The nearest live practice is git-native grant programs: the
[Web3 Foundation Grants-Program](https://github.com/w3f/Grants-Program),
[gno.land grants](https://github.com/gnolang/grants), and Secret Labs take
applications as markdown files submitted by pull request and reviewed
in-repo — real prior art for *proposals in git with PR review*, but the
artifact is narrative-only: no budget model, no funder rule packs, no
machine validation of content.

[OSCAL and compliance-trestle](https://github.com/oscal-compass/compliance-trestle)
are the strongest pattern-level prior art for C5: NIST schemas plus an
Apache-2.0 CLI under which security compliance documents — SSPs, catalogs —
are authored as markdown and JSON in git, validated and assembled by a tool
"designed to operate as a CI/CD pipeline running on top of compliance
artifacts in git" ([oscal.io/tools](https://oscal.io/tools/)). C5's residual
novelty is domain transfer — funder packs, budget caps, submission formats —
not the pattern. [Vale](https://vale.sh/) lints prose against YAML rule
packages in CI, used by the Grafana, Datadog, and Elastic docs teams;
grantkit's `check` is Vale-shaped with funder semantics — limits, required
sections, citations, budget caps.
[docassemble](https://docassemble.org/) (MIT license) assembles legal
documents from structured data through guided interviews in YAML, Python,
and Markdown, and the Suffolk LIT Lab's Assembly Line builds court forms on
it — documents-compiled-from-data is established in legal aid, without
budgets or funder rules.
[Catala](https://www.inria.fr/en/catala-software-dgfip-cnaf) transcribes
statutes into a verified DSL used with the French tax and benefits
administrations, and the
[Accord Project](https://docs.accordproject.org/docs/accordproject-slc.html)
makes contracts computable — together legitimizing C3's premise that
statute-to-code is a proven technique, which nobody has pointed at grant
budgets. Scientific manuscripts routinely render and check in CI (Quarto's
GitHub actions; Overleaf's git bridge), and policy-as-code engines such as
OPA evaluate structured inputs in CI for infrastructure and, via OSCAL
tooling, compliance data — with no application to grant forms or budgets
found.

The lane kills any claim that the *pattern* is new — trestle, Vale, and
docassemble own it. All six claims therefore rest on the grant-domain
objects: menus, fractions, funder packs, statutory rates. That is where the
sweep found no occupants.

## Compensation benchmarking

Does any tool compute loaded personnel costs from rules rather than
multipliers? Benchmarks turn out to be data products, and loading is either
a flat multiplier (grant practice) or a rules-based calculation in payroll
tools that never touches grant budgets and carries no benchmark provenance.

[Candid's Nonprofit Compensation Report](https://candid.org/nonprofit-compensation-report/)
studies executive compensation from IRS 990s — the 2025 edition covers 217k
records across 131k organizations, by position, budget band, and geography —
a benchmark *source*, and a static product.
[ERI's Nonprofit Comparables Assessor](https://www.erieri.com/nonprofitcomparablesassessor)
provides 990-derived comparables for 55 executive positions, supports
rebuttable-presumption-of-reasonableness documentation, and tracks
compensation against department budgets — benchmarks and audit rationale, no
statutory loading. [BLS OEWS](https://www.bls.gov/oes/) publishes wage
percentiles for roughly 830 occupations at national, state, and metro levels
— the standard citation for salary reasonableness in budget justifications,
and the provenance substrate C3 consumes; BLS publishes data, not
loaded-cost tooling. A genre of free
[true-cost-of-employee calculators](https://truetools.org/tools/employee-cost-calculator-usa)
computes employer FICA, FUTA, and SUTA from published parameters — some
[citing IRS Publication 15](https://jupid.com/payroll-tax-calculator) — plus
rule-of-thumb benefit and overhead percentages: partial prior art for C3's
computation, as throwaway web tools that handle no retirement-plan employer
caps as law, carry no benchmark provenance, and feed no budget artifact.
Production payroll engines — ADP, Gusto, et al. — compute actual employer
burden from encoded tax law every pay run, proving C3's computation feasible
and standard *post-hire*; no pre-award budgeting product surfaces it. And
grant practice itself budgets personnel as salary times a pooled fringe rate
— the Kuali and Cayuse mechanics above, NICRA culture — a multiplier
everywhere.

C3's parts all exist separately: benchmarks in Candid, ERI, and BLS;
rules-based loading in payroll engines and calculators; multipliers as the
incumbent. Composing them into a reproducible pre-award rate artifact with
provenance is the unoccupied square.

## Adjacent fields

Beyond the assigned lanes sit the closest conceptual neighbors — the ones a
referee will raise.

Government contracting solved structured cost buildup decades ago.
[Deltek ProPricer](https://www.propricer.com/), since 1984, generates FAR-15
and DCAA-defensible cost volumes from labor categories, indirect rate
structures, escalation, and CLINs — the strongest C1 neighbor in any
industry. The differences that keep C1 alive: closed; priced in
labor-category hours, not work items with completion evidence; no
cross-proposal allocation constraint; no CI or reproducibility story; wrap
rates as pooled multipliers (the C3 contrast again).
[BOEMax](https://www.projstream.com/basis-of-estimate-proposal-software-boemax)
keeps a central library of process templates — tasks, labor, materials — and
historical actuals, reused across proposals for consistent estimates: the
nearest neighbor to C4's menu, with no co-funding fractions (GovCon prices
one contract at a time), no sum-to-one gate, no funder-facing view.
Construction estimating — RSMeans data, Gordian — has compiled priced
work-item catalogs into bids for decades; the priced-menu-to-budget move is
ancient there, and the grant-domain novelty is a menu carrying
machine-checkable completion evidence and compiling under funder rule packs.

On the philanthropy side, the
[Philanthropy Data Commons](https://philanthropydatacommons.org/) is
open-source shared-data infrastructure — nonprofits enter organization and
proposal data once and multiple funders read it by API — C4-adjacent on the
*data* axis, but the shared objects are org profiles and proposal metadata,
not priced work items, with no budget or allocation semantics.
[Common grant applications](https://learning.candid.org/resources/knowledge-base/common-grant-application/)
— regional grantmaker associations, JustFund — are C4's inverse: N funders,
one *form*, no org-side substrate, no fractions.
[Braided-funding practice](https://ecbraiding.mathematica.org/) — the
[HHS/ASPE toolkit](https://www.aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/2021-08/EC_Braiding_Toolkit.pdf),
Mathematica's early-childhood braiding tool, TFAH's compendium — is C2 and
C4's conceptual ancestor in program finance: each funder pays its share, no
double-charging, enforced by guides, spreadsheets, and humans.

Three funder-facing surfaces frame C6.
[DonorsChoose](https://help.donorschoose.org/hc/en-us/articles/201936606-Vendor-pricing)
shows donors vendor-priced manifests of real line items, with price deltas
reconciled by policy — the nearest C6 neighbor, but the items are retail
SKUs, not the org's cost model, and there is no configurator over rates or
assumptions. [Open Collective](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/product/ledger)
makes a collective's full ledger — income, expenses, balance — public by
default: live *actuals*, not a forward cost model, with no selection or
toggle semantics. [Manifund](https://manifund.org/) runs open-source
regranting with public projects, funding goals, a public grant ledger, and
impact-certificate experiments — budgets as prose numbers, not models.

## Adjudication

No lane produced an occupant of the full stack. Two claims lost their loose
forms: C1's "computing budgets from data" is dead (Kuali, Cayuse, ProPricer,
construction estimating), and C3's "computing employer burden from rules" is
dead (payroll engines, web calculators); each survives only as stated — the
pure-function, work-item, CI-reproducible form of C1, and the composed,
provenance-carrying, pre-award form of C3. C5 is repositioned rather than
defended: its core — machine-encoded funder rules, automatic validation, a
structured error report — exists at scale in NIH ASSIST, and its pattern —
versioned rule packs validated in CI — exists in compliance-trestle; the
claim is the join, open and applicant-side and portable across funders. C2,
C4, and C6 stand as novel in their mechanisms, each with named ancestors:
the NIH overlap rule and effort certification for C2; BOE libraries, the
APD regime, and data commons for C4; itemized vendor pricing and live
ledgers for C6.

| Claim | Verdict | Nearest neighbors |
|---|---|---|
| C1 budget as compiled artifact | Partial prior art | [Kuali Research budget engine](https://kuali-research.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/115010656047-Proposal-Budget-Budget-Engine-Calculations) (rate-table autocalc; open-source ancestor frozen since 2017); [Deltek ProPricer](https://www.propricer.com/) (structured cost buildup) |
| C2 pre-award double-billing gate | Novel as a machine check; the invariant is old policy | [NIH commitment-overlap rule](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/policy/nihgps/HTML5/section_2/2.5.1_just-in-time_procedures.htm), staff-resolved at award; [Huron ECC](https://finance.uw.edu/pafc/effort-reporting/ecc-system/ecc-overview) post-award certification |
| C3 rule-derived personnel rates | Partial prior art | [Payroll-tax calculators](https://jupid.com/payroll-tax-calculator) (rules-based loading, no provenance, post-hire); [pooled fringe rates](https://support.cayuse.com/hc/en-us/articles/115013737108-Adding-Fringe-Rates-and-Benefits-in-Proposals-S2S) (the incumbent) |
| C4 funder-as-view | Novel as a mechanism; ancestors are copy-forward reuse | [BOEMax](https://www.projstream.com/basis-of-estimate-proposal-software-boemax) estimate library; [Philanthropy Data Commons](https://philanthropydatacommons.org/) (one dataset, many funders) |
| C5 versioned funder packs + CI + status artifact | Exists (core, closed); partial (open, applicant-side packaging) | [NIH ASSIST](https://www.era.nih.gov/about-era/other-services/validations) business-rule validation; [compliance-trestle](https://github.com/oscal-compass/compliance-trestle) rule packs in git + CI |
| C6 funder-facing configurator | Novel; thinnest neighbor set, adoption untested | [DonorsChoose](https://help.donorschoose.org/hc/en-us/articles/201936606-Vendor-pricing) itemized vendor pricing; [Open Collective](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/product/ledger) live public ledger |

: Claim × verdict × nearest neighbor, from the 2026-08-14 sweep. {#tbl-verdicts}

Two closing notes. The exact phrases "grants as code" and "CI for grants"
were unclaimed as of the 2026-08 sweep — no tool, paper, or product uses
either for grant applications, and the nearest live practice is
[crypto grant programs run as markdown pull requests](https://github.com/w3f/Grants-Program).
And the verdicts rest on absence of evidence in a US-centric,
English-language sweep: *novel* means no prior art found, not proven absent.

# The pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

<!-- verify against final v0.3 code before publication -->

grantkit 0.3 introduces the budget model: three YAML document types, a
pure-function engine, a set of gates, and a new CLI verb, `budget`,
alongside the existing pack verbs (`check` and `build` among them). The
design keeps a strict engine/data boundary: grantkit ships the schemas, the
engine, and synthetic fixtures; an organization's menus, rates, and
selections live in the organization's own repositories. Everything is
stateless and local-first — no network calls, no model in the loop — and
compilation is deterministic: the same inputs produce the same bytes, with
money held as floats internally and rendered as whole dollars only at
output.

## Three documents

**The menu** (`grantkit-menu/v0`) is the organization's priced work-item
catalog. It carries org-level economics — named overheads such as a
fiscal-sponsorship rate, each with provenance — and named unit costs, each a
unit price with a derivation string and a provenance list. Every item has an
id; a type (free vocabulary, with recommended values program-coverage,
platform, research-eval, field, and org-base); a title; a one-sentence
statement of what it is; machine-checkable completion evidence; a status
(shipped, in-flight, or planned); a dependency list whose ids must resolve;
and a non-empty provenance list. An item's resourcing block prices it in any
of five ways, at least one required: FTE-months by role (roles must exist in
the rates file), unit counts (names must exist in the unit costs), flat
contract dollars, recurring dollars per year (prorated over a selection's
window), or a flat amount (the shape org-base blocks use). A flat or
contract amount can declare `overhead_included: true`, meaning the amount
already contains org overheads and the selection-level overhead must not
apply again; the default is false. The flag exists because upstream org
models emit fee-inclusive totals — @sec-case shows what happens without it.

**The rates file** (`grantkit-rates/v0`) is a contract with a rates
provider, not a place to type numbers. It must name its provider and
version, its generation date, and its currency, and may carry a scenario id,
a jurisdiction, and a prose description of the method. The reference
provider is eggnest-employer, which derives loaded cost as base salary plus
employer payroll taxes computed from encoded law (via PolicyEngine), plus an
employer retirement contribution applied as a rate against base and capped
by statute, plus a configured benefits schedule. Each role carries a
required annual loaded cost, a recommended base, an optional SOC code, an
optional component breakdown, and an optional benchmark. Every component
states its basis from a closed vocabulary — computed, configured, or assumed
— and its source; the benchmark block carries market provenance, for example
a BLS OEWS percentile with its exact series and value. grantkit validates
presence and types; it does not recompute a provider's law-based numbers —
that is the provider's job, under the provider's tests. Two advisory
warnings police the seam. A load-factor check flags any role whose
loaded-to-base ratio falls below 1.05 ("loaded equals base — pasted base as
loaded?") or above 2.0 — a bug class observed in the wild, when three roles
in a seeded menu carried base salary pasted as loaded cost. A components
check flags any breakdown that misses the stated loaded cost by more than a
dollar.

**A selection** (`grantkit-selection/v0`) is a proposal: an id, a funder, a
status from a closed vocabulary (draft, live, awarded, withdrawn, declined),
an optional advisory target, a required window in months, an optional
org-base allocation (an item that must be of type org-base, with a fraction
between zero and one), and an ordered list of selected items, each with a
co-funding fraction. Explicit zero fractions are preserved and meaningful:
an item selected at fraction 0.0 with a note is *declared, not billed* — the
funder sees that the work exists in the plan and that this proposal pays
none of it.

A portfolio directory holds the menu, the rates file, and a `selections/`
directory of proposals (a single selection file beside the menu also works
for one-proposal setups). A grant project can bind itself to one selection
through its `grant.yaml`, pointing at the portfolio and naming the
selection.

## The engine

Compilation is two pure functions. Item cost: labor is the sum over roles of
FTE-months divided by twelve times the role's loaded annual cost; units are
count times unit price; contract and flat amounts pass through; these sum to
a one-time cost, with recurring dollars carried separately. Selection cost:
each selected item contributes its fraction times its one-time cost, plus
its fraction times its recurring cost prorated by the window (months over
twelve); the org base contributes its fraction times the org-base item's
one-time cost, deliberately not window-prorated — flat blocks are priced as
blocks, matching upstream practice; overhead applies the org's rate to every
component except those whose amount came from a field flagged
`overhead_included`, which makes the fee idempotent by construction; the
total is work plus base plus overhead, and when the selection declares a
target, the compilation reports fit as total over target.

## The gates

`grantkit budget --check` runs the integrity gates over a whole portfolio
and exits nonzero on errors (1 for findings, 2 for an unreadable
portfolio). The errors: schema violations in any of the three documents;
references that do not resolve — a selection naming a missing item, an item
naming a missing role or unit, a dependency naming a missing item;
dependency cycles, found by depth-first search in deterministic order;
fractions outside zero to one; an org-base reference to an item that is not
of type org-base; the same item listed twice in one selection; and the C2
gate, `cofunding_over_allocated`, which for every item sums fractions
across all selections with status live or awarded and fails if the sum
exceeds one (with a 1e-9 tolerance), naming each contributing selection and
its fraction in the message. The same rule applies to org-base fractions
per org-base item. Draft, withdrawn, and declined selections are excluded
by design: the invariant binds simultaneous live applications, drafts are
free to over-plan, and the gate fires when they go live.

The warnings: a funded item depends on work that is neither shipped,
in-flight, nor funded in any live or awarded selection — the proposal
assumes work nobody has funded; the compiled total exceeds the declared
target (advisory — a target is an ask, not a cap); and the rates-contract
heuristics above. Inside a grant project bound to a selection, the funder
pack's budget caps also apply to the compiled total as errors, reusing the
existing cap identifiers, with annual caps approximated as total times
twelve over the window months (documented as an approximation).

## The budget verb

`grantkit budget` prints the compilation as tables: a summary, per-item
costs, and per-role personnel. `--json` emits the full structured
compilation. `--output` writes a markdown budget document: a header stating
the selection, funder, window, status, and a generated-from line naming the
menu and the rates provider, version, and date — the reproducibility
statement; a selected-items table with fractions, item costs, and funded
shares; a personnel table with fraction-weighted FTE-months, loaded annual
rates, and a benchmark column when the rates carry benchmarks; and a
category summary — labor, units, contract, flat, recurring prorated, org
base, overhead, total — with a target-fit line. `--narrative` appends a
narrative skeleton: for each funded item, its title, what it is, its
completion evidence, and its cost line; then a budget-justification
skeleton per role, with a benchmark-provenance sentence where present. The
narrative renders from the compiled objects only — no generated prose
beyond connective boilerplate.

## Continuous integration

A repository that holds a portfolio, or a grant project bound to a
selection, runs `grantkit check` and `grantkit budget` in CI. Inside a
bound project, the selection gates and funder caps fold into the same
findings stream and exit-code semantics the pack checks already use, so an
application repo fails to build when its budget breaks an invariant exactly
as it fails when a required section is missing. Determinism makes the diff
meaningful: a changed rate or fraction shows up as a changed table and
nothing else. The C2 invariant re-verifies on every push — including pushes
that edit *other* proposals, which is the point: the gate binds the
portfolio, not the file being edited. The funder sees the same numbers the
org plans by.

The pipeline demonstrates C1 on itself. The test suite compiles a synthetic
portfolio — three roles (one with a full component breakdown and benchmark,
one base-only, one loaded-only), six items (an org-base block with overhead
included, a unit-priced item, a recurring item, a dependency chain, a
shipped item), and three selections (two live selections sharing an item at
0.5 each, a draft over-planner, and an explicit-zero declaration) — and
asserts that two runs produce identical output. Any budget table this paper
ships regenerates from that fixture via `grantkit budget`; rendering the
paper is itself a check. The configurator (C6) is a surface over the same
compiled objects; @sec-case describes its one live use.

# Case study {#sec-case}

<!-- Reconcile pass: every figure in this section re-verifies against
ballmer-proposal-2026 PR #17 / CAMPAIGN.md before publication. -->

The pipeline's first live run was an August 2026 diligence sprint at The
Axiom Foundation, presented here with funders unnamed. The substrate was one
rates scenario plus a menu of 24 priced work items seeded from the sprint's
diligence corpus. Figures are from the sprint's working records.

In one evening, a bottoms-up org model derived four coherent org shapes —
$21.2 million to $37.8 million over five years — from the one
rates-plus-items substrate. Each shape is a selection, so a changed rate or
assumption regenerates all four together. The same substrate then priced a
$2 million concept note, and the first selection came out at 134% of target
— a 34% overshoot exposed before submission, so the trim happened in the
org's own repository rather than in a funder's diligence. And it expressed
a three-level funder structure as three nested views over the same menu,
which became funder-level presets: the same items, different fractions and
windows, consistent by construction.

The compilation also surfaced a decision the spreadsheet workflow had
buried. One leadership pricing question — a levy versus a full-price
posture for attestation — had sat implicit for weeks; pricing the menu
forced it into the open, as a choice the organization had to make rather
than a number that varied with whichever spreadsheet was open.

One discovery is worth stating mechanically, because it is the shape of
error this compilation catches. An upstream org-cost block already carried
a 7% fiscal-sponsorship fee inside its total. An ad-hoc pricer multiplied
that block by 1.07 again. In the typed substrate, the block is a flat
amount with `overhead_included: true`, so the engine exempts it from
selection-level overhead and the fee applies exactly once, by construction.
Porting the model removed a $99,750 phantom and moved one live view from
134% to 129% of its target. The remaining overshoot was real scope to trim,
not arithmetic — a distinction a hand-built budget cannot make about
itself.

# What this does not solve {#sec-limits}

The pipeline does not write the proposal. Narrative quality is untouched:
the prose is still written, by people or by models; the pipeline only
guarantees that the prose sits on true numbers. Relationship work is
untouched. The menu can be gamed by its own organization — garbage items
in, plausible budget out; the gates check consistency, not wisdom. Funder
adoption of configurators is untested beyond the one live diligence in
@sec-case. Rule-derived rates currently cover United States federal and
state payroll and retirement law only. And mechanically, v0.3 prorates
recurring costs over a single window — no multi-year phasing — and assumes
single-currency portfolios.

# Availability {#sec-availability}

<!-- MAX DECISION (pre-publication): eggnest-employer is a PRIVATE repo as
of 2026-08-14, so "all components are open source" would be false. Either
publish eggnest-employer before this paper ships or keep the softened
wording below ("public release is pending"); the abstract claims only the
engine and schemas as open source for the same reason. Org data repos
(menus, selections) are also private and stay that way; the synthetic
fixture is the public reproduction path. -->

grantkit is on PyPI under the MIT license; the menu, rates, and selection
schemas and the budget engine ship with it, along with the synthetic
fixture portfolio, so the compilation demonstrated here reproduces end to
end without private data. The reference rates provider, eggnest-employer,
is not yet public; its release is pending. Organization menus and
selections live in organization repositories and remain private — the
case-study figures in @sec-case come from those records, and the mechanics
they exercise are the same ones the fixture exercises in the open. The
paper itself will be embedded at grantkit.io once public.
